internal_claims.claim: Northbridge ran full diligence on an EGS company internally codenamed 'Thermalis' (developer using directional drilling adapted from oil & gas to enable geothermal outside traditional volcanic/tectonic-boundary regions) in connection with its Series B raise within the past year, and passed.

The firm explicitly recorded that its pass on Thermalis was NOT due to technical skepticism about the EGS approach broadly - its technical advisor assessed the underlying directional-drilling technology as 'reasonably de-risked' given its oil & gas heritage - and the memo flags that the pass was thesis-specific to that one company, not a signal against enhanced geothermal as a sub-segment.

The actual stated reason for passing on Thermalis was not present in any retrieved passage from this document - only the negative (what did NOT drive the pass) was captured, so the affirmative rationale remains undocumented in what was surfaced here.

During the Thermalis diligence cycle, Northbridge informally tracked two other earlier-stage (seed/Series A) EGS developers without running full diligence on either, and observed both were pursuing a similar directional-drilling approach, suggesting this method may be converging as the dominant technical approach in the EGS sub-segment rather than being one company's differentiated edge.

In the firm's quarterly cross-sector scan, inbound deal flow tagged 'enhanced geothermal' was roughly flat quarter-over-quarter, but the average stage of inbound shifted later (fewer seed-stage intros, more Series B+), which the firm interpreted as a possible sign the sub-segment is maturing past its earliest, most speculative phase.

Multiple LPs have asked Northbridge about its exposure to 'firm, dispatchable clean power' as a category spanning both advanced nuclear and enhanced geothermal, framed as a hedge against intermittent renewables' grid integration challenges; the firm notes this cross-sub-segment 'dispatchability' framing from LPs is relatively new.

The quarterly sector scan is explicitly caveated as directional and unverified, drawing on inbound deal flow, LP conversations, and informal market chatter rather than confirmed data - and separately warns that the firm's own inbound deal-flow patterns are a lagging, self-selected signal that should be checked against external published data before being treated as representative of the sector.

Gridline Storage Systems (an existing Northbridge portfolio company in grid-scale battery storage, not itself a geothermal company) reported via its CEO that utility customers in at least two recent conversations specifically named advanced nuclear or geothermal as the assumed firm-generation source they want storage deployments modeled alongside, rather than treating storage as a standalone intermittency solution - taken by the firm as a demand-side signal relevant to (though not direct evidence within) the geothermal sub-segment.

The firm explicitly caveats that this Gridline customer-conversation signal is anecdotal (one portfolio company's customer conversations, not a systematic survey) and should not be treated as a quantified market signal on its own for geothermal or advanced nuclear.

external_claims.claim: Fervo Energy raised a $462 million Series E funding round in December 2025 to accelerate geothermal development and meet surging energy demand.
Fervo Energy has raised over $1.5 billion in total funding as of mid-2026, including the $462 million round closed in December 2025.
Sage Geosystems closed a $97 million Series B funding round, announced around January 21, 2026, to support deployment of its Pressure Geothermal technology.
Sage Geosystems has raised $142 million total to date as of its $97M Series B round, per PitchBook company data.
Quaise Energy raised $134 million in the first close of a Series B round, announced July 7, 2026, to build what it describes as the world's first superhot geothermal power plant.
Quaise Energy has closed $230 million in total funding to date as of its Series B first close in July 2026.
Quaise Energy previously raised a $21 million Series A1 financing round, announced in March 2024, led by Prelude Ventures and Safar Partners.
In November 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy merged its geothermal office with its fossil energy office, creating a new Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy office.
The typical timeline for permitting a geothermal project in the U.S. can take between 5 and 10 years, according to the Niskanen Center.
Fervo Energy announced a 70% reduction in geothermal drilling time, with drilling costs across the first four horizontal wells at its Cape project falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million per well.

According to a May 2026 ITIF publication, a single enhanced geothermal well costs $5 million to $10 million to drill, with per-well costs having fallen from a prior range as drilling rates have improved.
Ormat Technologies announced on February 17, 2026 the signing of a geothermal portfolio power purchase agreement of up to 150 MW to support Google's data center operations through NV Energy.

As of September 2025, Fervo Energy's initial 100-MW geothermal installation was poised to start delivering power to the grid in 2026, with an additional 400 MW planned, under partnerships with large tech companies.
A $1 billion geothermal data center project in Kenya intended to power Microsoft operations was paused due to insufficient national energy capacity to support the site, as reported in July 2026.

Enhanced geothermal systems have faced delays attributed to slow permitting and transmission interconnection processes, and in one case a mismatch between the paucity of lease auctions and demand, according to a Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy roundtable summary.
